title: Pauri 20, meaning: what washes the mind
hookLine: water washes dirty hands and soap soiled clothes; a mind soiled by wrong is dyed clean by love of the Name; as you sow, you reap (Japji 20)

cards: Some stains come out with water. Some need soap and a good scrub. And some things a person did years ago sit on them like a stain no laundry will lift: a cruel word to a brother, a friend let down.
A shower doesn't touch it; it's still there at two in the morning. Pauri 20 walks right up to that stain, one step at a time.

teach.h: WATER FOR HANDS, SOAP FOR CLOTHES.
teach.b: Pauri 20 climbs a little ladder. Step one, yesterday's: when hands, feet and body are dirty, water washes the dust off. Step two, in paraphrase: when clothes are soiled, even badly, you apply soap and wash them clean.

Step three, and here the stanza turns: when the mind is soiled by wrongdoing, it is washed by the love of the Name. The original has a lovely word there: oh dhopai naavai kai rang. Rang is color, dye.

teach.h: THE MIND, DYED IN THE NAME.
teach.b: The mind isn't only scrubbed; it's dyed, soaked through in the color of the Name, the way cloth takes on a new color in the vat.
In Sikh writing, being dyed in the Name, rang, is a recurring picture of love that goes all the way through. Then the stanza keeps this from being too easy.
Virtuous and sinner, it says, aren't just labels people say. What you do, again and again, is written down and goes with you.
And the line behind today's carry, in the original: aape beej aape hee khaahu. You yourself sow, and you yourself eat. Whatever seed you plant is the harvest you'll live on.
Nanak says we come and go by the Hukam, the divine order.
So two things stand side by side. The Name can dye even a stained mind clean. And actions still matter; you eat what you plant.
Grace and responsibility, in one stanza, and it doesn't let go of either.

how: Pauri 20 is recited in Japji Sahib each morning; Sikhs often speak of being dyed in the Name, rang, and quote aape beej aape hee khaahu to say that each person reaps what they sow.

o: a stain that won't wash out of the mind
soap that scrubs the dirt from clothes
color, dye that soaks all the way through

games.q: the ladder of Pauri 20 — tap the pairs.

s: Pauri 20 says a stained mind can be washed with water
water is for hands; the mind is dyed clean by the love of the Name.
Pauri 20 says you eat what you yourself sow
rang in Pauri 20 means color or dye
the mind is soaked through, like cloth in a vat.

games.q: your mind carries a stain no shower will lift. what does Pauri 20 say washes it?
o: the love of the Name, which dyes it clean.
games.why: oh dhopai naavai kai rang: it's washed in the color of the Name. and still, you eat what you sow.

practice: If you can, wash your hands now, slowly, feeling the water, the soap, each finger; if you can't get to a sink, rub your palms together as if washing them.
As you do, let one small thing you'd like to be washed clean of be there with the water, without dwelling on it. Then sit, hands resting, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Rang. Color, dye: the mind soaked through in the color of the Name. Water washes hands, soap washes clothes, and the love of the Name dyes the mind clean. And you eat what you sow.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 20: you yourself sow, and you yourself eat.

carryVoice: Your line: as you sow. The Name dyes the mind, and the harvest is still yours. That's day one hundred ninety-four.
